# Introduction

This page provides an overview of building and managing dimension and fact tables within an Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW). You’ll learn how to create sequences, tables, and stored procedures, as well as how to manage the data flow from staging to the final EDW layer. It also includes guidance on using synonyms and integrating SSIS packages for a structured and optimized data warehouse process.

[[_TOC_]]

---
# EDW

## EDW (Model)

The EDW layer is the largest layer, and this is where most of the work with loading, transforming, validating, and building a star schema takes place. The natural keys from the source are mapped to EDW keys and surrogate keys, with handling of changing dimensions.

Framework Components in EDW layer

| Type | Name | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **schema** | archive | Used to access tables from ‘archive’ via synonyms in the EDW database. |
|  | datamart |  |
|  | dimension |  |
|  | fact |  |
|  | management |  |
|  | mapping |  |
|  | stage |  |
|  | system |  |
|  | template |  |
| **synonym** | archive |  |
|  | datamart |  |
|  | management |  |
| **sequences** | dimension |  |
| **stored procedures** | dimension.CreateUnknownEntities |  |
|  | system.TSQL_SimpleFieldList | Helper functions to generate SQL code for select, assign, and compare, optimizing stored procedures. |
|  | system.TSQL_AssignFieldList |  |
|  | system.TSQL_CompareFieldList |  |
|  | system.DataMartTableInsertMaster | Adjusted whenever a table is added to the DataMart. |
|  | system.DataMartTableInsert | Not to be used directly; used by ‘system.DataMartInsertMaster’. |
|  | system.SSISpackagesInsertMaster | Adjusted when adding a new SSIS package to EDW main packages. |
|  | system.SSISpackagesInsert | Not to be used directly; used by ‘system.SSISpackagesInsertMaster’. |
|  | system.GetNums | Returns a temp table with numbers between specified min and max. |

## EDW: Naming Conventions

It is important to follow a standard naming convention for objects. This naming convention is used in the EDW layer:

| Object type | Standard | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **DIMENSION** | `[archive].[<source_system>_<source_table>]` | `[archive].[PRISME_LEDGERTABLE]` |
| Sequence EK | `[dimension].[EK_<entity>]` | `[dimension].[EK_Konto]` |
| Mapping table | `[mapping].[<entity>_<source_system>]` | `[mapping].[Konto_PRISME]` |
| Mapping stored procedure | `[mapping].[Update_<entity>_<source_system>]` | `[mapping].[Update_Konto_PRISME]` |
| Stage table | `[stage].[Dimension<entity>]` | `[stage].[DimensionKonto]` |
| Stage stored procedure | `[dimension].[Insert_<entity>]` | `[dimension].[Insert_Konto]` |
| Sequence SK | `[dimension].[SK_<entity>]` | `[dimension].[SK_Konto]` |
| Dimension table | `[dimension].[<entity>]` | `[dimension].[Konto]` |
| Dimension stored procedure | `[dimension].[Insert_<entity>]` | `[dimension].[Insert_Konto]` |
| **FACT** | `[archive].[<source_system>_<source_table>]` | `[archive].[PRISME_LEDGERTRANS]` |  
| Stage table | `[stage].[Fact<entity>]` | `[stage].[FactOekonomiPostering]` |  
| Stage stored procedure | `[stage].[Insert_Fact<entity>]` | `[stage].[Insert_FactOekonomiPostering]` |  
| Fact table | `[fact].[<entity>]` | `[fact].[OekonomiPostering]` |  
| Fact stored procedure | `[fact].[Insert_<entity>]` | `[fact].[Insert_OekonomiPostering]` |

## EDW: DW Fields

This table lists the various DW fields found in the EDW layer across mapping, dimension, and fact tables.

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **DW_EK_** | The unique translation of a natural key from the source system to a running number in EDW. This is a 1:1 mapping. Note – if the source delivers a changing dimension, the EK key will be the same as the SK key, since the changing dimension is already represented in the mapping table and DW_ValidFrom is part of the key in the mapping table. |
| **DW_SK_** | When the final dimension table is created (`[dimension].[<entity>]`), the EK key is converted to an SK key. Typically 1:1, but multiple SK keys per EK key can be created if it is a changing dimension.|
| **DW_SK_<entity_role>** | Role-based dimensions can occur – especially for dates. For example, there can be several date fields referencing the dimension.Date. These should then be named in the fact table as `DW_SK_BookingDate`, `DW_SK_DueDate`, etc. |
| **DW_ValidDate** | This is a date field and must contain the date value used in the join between dimension and fact to find the SK key. |
| **DW_ArchiveID** | This field is carried forward from the archive table in the staging layer so that the data origin can be traced. The value can be ‘0’ if the table is aggregated over archive data – e.g., by a distinct or group by operation. |
| **DW_ValidFrom** | Used together with `DW_ValidTo` to join the fact table with the dimension to ‘capture’ the correct SK key based on an EK key. For non-changing dimensions, this field assumes a minimum value. |
| **DW_ValidTo** | See `DW_ValidFrom`. |
| **DW_IsCurrent** | Indicates with the value ‘1’ whether the record is the newest version in case of a changing dimension. |
| **DW_Audit_Insert** | This field should have the same value as `DW_Audit` when the record is inserted into the table. |
| **DW_Audit_Update** | This field should only be assigned the same value as `DW_Audit` when the record is updated. |
| **DW_Audit** | ‘Audit’ is a sequential number extracted when the job starts. That is, all records affected in the same run/batch receive the same number. This field must be filled for both ‘Insert’ and ‘Update’ transactions. |

## EDW: Data Cleaning

Data cleansing takes place in one specific part of the architecture – namely in the **stage** layer for dimensions and facts. This means the layer between **archive** and the final dimension or fact tables. (See **Dimension: Stored procedure for stage table** or **Fact: Stored procedure for stage table**.)
Data cleansing involves the following types of cleaning:
*   Handling of NULL values. These are replaced by blank, 0, or for dates ‘19000101’.
    
*   Handling of ‘unknown’ values between dimension and fact.
    
*   Handling of ‘blank’ values in fact tables relative to a dimension.
    
*   Handling of -1 and -2 values:

| Value | Description |
| --- | --- |
| -1 | Means ‘Unknown’. If a record in a fact table points to a dimension value of -1, this means the corresponding value is unknown in the dimension. We do not create the unknown values. Example: In this fact table, there are rows where `DW_SK_Maskin` is -1. This means unknown. By using the column `DW_ArchiveID`, it is possible to find the source record and observe which value is missing. See below, where the value ‘000’ exists in the transaction but not in the dimension data. There is no automatic logging of which values are unknown ![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-4078a208-2bbc-4785-82c1-d39d995e6f2e.png) .|
||![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-3eb6add5-8eb6-4cba-a828-bb3df6134707.png) |
| -2 | Means ‘blank’. In the example above for -1, there are several columns with -2. This means, for example, that many records do not have a value in the column ‘Department’ or ‘Purpose’, so the fact table points to -2 to keep the data consistent. |

# Dimension

## Dimension: General

The diagram below illustrates the flow that occurs from **stage** to **EDW** in a dimension.
![image.png](/.attachments/image-18b7895d-1ae0-4d25-b242-8375f9f7a983.png)
A typical flow in the framework is that data from **archive** forms the basis for a **mapping** table (more on this later). A **stage** table is built with cleansed data – also from **archive** – with renamed columns, adjusted data types, possibly new constructed columns, and a **mapping key** called the EK key. Once the **stage** table is ready, the final dimension table can be created, where EK keys are converted to SK keys – handling changing dimensions, deleted, and updated records.

In very simple versions of dimensions, the **stage** layer can be omitted, but this is not recommended since the hard work still needs to be done somewhere between **archive** and **dim**. Doing this work from **archive** to **stage** makes the last step quick and if more advanced logic is needed later, the staging is already in place.

In other situations where the final table is sourced from multiple **archive** tables, the **stage** layer should always be created first, so the final step of building the dimension only handles SK keys, changing dimensions, and deleted records.

Below is a list of elements involved in building a dimension in the EDW and their function/meaning:
| Object | Example | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synonym | `[archive].[PRISME_LEDGERTABLE]` | Creates a reference to the mentioned table from the stage database (DSA) to the EDW database, so the table is recognized by T-SQL and IntelliSense as part of the database. |
| Sequence EK | `[dimension].[EK_Konto]` | Counter for sequential numbering of the EK key for the object. Used in the mapping table. |
| Mapping table | `[mapping].[Konto_PRISME]` | Contains information about mapping the natural key (one or more fields) from the source to an EK key. |
| Mapping stored procedure | `[mapping].[Update_Konto_PRISME]` | Updates the mapping table via the synonym from the source. |
| Stage table | `[stage].[DimensionKonto]` | The almost final dimension with fields from the source plus new generated fields. The table has final naming and data types. Natural keys are translated to EK keys and the table is ready to be inserted or merged into the final dimension table. |
| Stage stored procedure | `[dimension].[Insert_Konto]` | Stored procedure that creates the stage dimension table. |
| Sequence SK | `[dimension].[SK_Konto]` | Counter for sequential numbering of the SK key for the object. Used on the dimension table. |
| Dimension table | `[dimension].[Konto]` | The final dimension table where data from the stage table is merged, and history is created if applicable. Note: dimension tables are never deleted. |
| Dimension stored procedure | `[dimension].[Insert_Konto]` | Creates the final dimension – including creation of -1 and -2 values. |

## Dimension: Quick-link
![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-ea832e58-4d1b-4344-9c63-e483e7739d9e.png) 

## Dimension: Mapping Table

First, create a **sequence** object for the `[DW_EK_xxxxx]` key in the **mapping** table to generate a sequential number series. This is done as follows:

Copy the file  
`..\src\sql\Templates\Sequence\dimension.EK_DimTable.Sequence.sql`  
to the correct folder and replace `DimTable` with the name of your dimension both in the filename and inside the code of the file.

A **sequence** performs better than an **IDENTITY** column, and the advantage is that when there are multiple mapping tables for the same dimension, all mapping tables must use the same sequence to avoid conflicts in the EK key.

Next, create a mapping table based on the template shown below. Note that the naming and data types reflect the source system – including case sensitivity and the same key as in the source – plus the field `[DW_ValidFrom]`.

Copy the file  
`..\src\sql\Templates\Tables\mapping.DimTable_SourceSystem.Table.sql`  
to the correct folder and replace `DimTable` and `SourceSystem` with the name of your dimension and the source system, both in the filename and inside the code of the file. Adjust the key fields as needed.

## Dimension: Synonym to Archive Table

You need to create a **synonym** for the **stage** database so that tables from **archive** are treated as natural tables within the EDW database. This is required to use tables from multiple databases within the same stored procedure. An added benefit is that IntelliSense works across databases.
The file should contain all synonyms to archive tables. First, copy the file  
`..\src\sql\Templates\Synonyms\archive.SourceSystem_SynonymScript.sql`  
to the correct folder and replace `SourceSystem` with your source system name.  
Inside the file, create one line per synonym, replacing `NameOfArchiveTable` with the correct table name.


## Dimension: Stored Procedure for Mapping Table

Copy the file  
`..\src\sql\Templates\Procedures\mapping.UpdateDimTable_SourceSystem.StoredProcedure.sql`  
to the correct folder and replace `DimTable` and `SourceSystem` with the name of your dimension and source system in both the filename and inside the code. Adjust the key fields as needed.

Save the stored procedure and execute it to test.


## Dimension: Stage Table

The staging table is the intermediate table where an EK key is assigned via mapping, and the naming and data types are tailored to the final EDW structure.
The result is a table that can be easily **MERGED** with the final dimension table, where the EK key is converted to an SK key (surrogate key).

Copy the file  
`..\src\sql\Templates\Tables\stage.DimensionDimTable.Table.sql`  
to the correct folder and replace `DimTable` with your dimension name in both filename and code. Add all columns in the code.

**Note:**
*   Column naming and data types must be final for the dimension – **no Danish letters (æ, ø, å)** in column names.
    
*   All columns must be **NOT NULL**.
    
Try to name key fields ending with `ID` and descriptions with names like `Description`, `Text`, or `Name`. It is important that the associated description clearly indicates which dimension it belongs to, not just generic names like `Text` or `Name`. Examples:
| Key Field | Description Field |
| --- | --- |
| StatusID | StatusText |
| CivilStatusID | CivilStatusDescription |
| AgeID | AgeText |
| MoveLocationID | MoveLocationText |

## Dimension: Stored Procedure for Stage Table

This stored procedure handles all necessary casting and conversions. It is also where new fields are created/calculated, along with all logic typically done in an SSIS package, so the result in the stage table is ready just before loading into the final dimension table.

Copy the file  
`..\src\sql\Templates\Procedures\stage.Insert_DimensionDimTable.StoredProcedure.sql`  
to the correct folder and replace `DimTable` with your dimension name in both filename and code. Add all columns in the code.

**Important:** There must be **no NULL values** in the stage table.

## Dimension: Dimension Table
First, a sequence must be created for the dimension table to generate continuous numbering of the SK key (surrogate key). This is done as described below. Note that a sequence can easily be used by multiple tables if necessary.

Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Sequence\dimension.SK_DimTable.Sequence.sql` to the correct folder and replace 'DimTable' with the name of your dimension in both the filename and in the code in the file.

The dimension table is created as follows:
Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Tables\dimension.DimTable.Table.sql` to the correct folder and replace 'DimTable' with the name of your dimension in both the filename and in the code in the file.

Next, insert the new fields – possibly by scripting the corresponding stage table and doing a copy/paste. The fields must be NOT NULL, and char fields must be at least 6 characters long to accommodate 'unknown' and 'blank' values.

## Dimension: Stored Procedure for the Dimension Table
Creating the final dimension table can vary in complexity, and this will be reflected in the stored procedure. It can be a Type 1 or Type 2 dimension. For both types, the dimension table is NEVER deleted; only insert/update or actual merge operations are performed.

Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Procedures\dimension.Insert_DimTable.StoredProcedure.sql` to the correct folder and replace 'DimTable' with the name of your dimension in both the filename and in the code in the file. Adjust it with all columns.

**Note** – this template includes an example of both Type 1 and Type 2 dimensions, so some code must be adjusted, and other parts should be deleted or commented out.

**Brief description of the logic for Type 1:**
Update the records that have changed attributes. The comparison is done for all records where `[DW_IsCurrent] = 1`, compared against the stage table using the EK key.
Insert the items from the stage table that do not exist in the dimension table.

**Brief description of the logic for Type 2:**
Create a temporary table containing the EK keys (entities) that have changed, based on the same logic as point 1 in Type 1. This table is generated by comparing all records where `[DW_IsCurrent] = 1`, matched with the stage table using the EK key. The temp table also includes a ChangeDate. Where that date comes from is not always clear, but in the template it is set to today’s date.

For the records in the dimension table that are in the newly generated temp table, set `IsCurrent = 0` and `ValidTo` to `ChangeDate - 1`.
Insert the new records in the same way as in Type 1.
All new records where the EK key exists in the temp table will have `ValidFrom = ChangeDate`.

**Note** - this template for inserting a dimension automatically calls a stored procedure `CreateUnknownEntities`, which inserts -1 and -2 values into the dimension.

## Dimension: SSIS flow
The final step is to add the package to the SSIS flow, which is executed by the standard SSIS project for running the EDW layer.

This is done by modifying the stored procedure `system.SSISpackagesInsertMaster` and adding a line like this:

`EXECUTE [system].[SSISpackagesInsert]  @Area,'<entity>','Dimension',1`

# Fact

## Fact: General
The construction of a fact table follows the same principles as a dimension, with the exception of the mapping step, although the result of the mapping is used in the creation of the final fact.

The diagram shown below illustrates the flow that occurs from stage to EDW for a fact.
![image.png](/.attachments/image-53a88611-c9ab-4102-b191-1f1414472e1c.png)

| **Object** | **Name (example)** | **Description** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synonym** | `[archive].[PRISME_LEDGERTRANS]` | Creates a reference to the mentioned table from the stage database (DSA) to the EDW database, so that the table is perceived by T-SQL and built-in IntelliSense as part of the database. |
| **Stage table** | `[stage].[FactOekonomiPostering]` | Construction of the fact table using naming consistent with the final fact table. EK (business) keys are added by joining with mapping tables, and special calculations/filtering are performed. |
| **Stage stored procedure** | `[stage].[Insert_FactOekonomiPostering]` | Stored procedure for building the stage table. |
| **Fact table** | `[fact].[OekonomiPostering]` | The final fact table that contains all history. If possible, it will be updated using a MERGE command from the stage table. |
| **Fact stored procedure** | `[fact].[Insert_OekonomiPostering]` | Stored procedure for building the final fact table, where EK keys are translated into SK (surrogate) keys using a date and data from the stage table. |

## Fact: Quick-link

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-f93f9331-0455-440d-b281-fa3d30ae012c.png) 

## Fact: Synonym for the archive table

A synonym must be created for the 'stage' database so that the table from 'archive' is included as a natural table in the EDW database. This is a requirement in order to use tables from multiple databases within the same stored procedure. An additional benefit is that IntelliSense works across databases.

## Fact: Stage table
Staging of the fact table before it is merged or inserted into the final fact table serves several purposes. Data is prepared as a sort of draft before the final fact in terms of data cleansing, calculation of new columns, and mapping of production keys to EK keys. Since the step – like all other steps – is performed as a stored procedure, there is full flexibility, but use the templates as a starting point.

Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Tables\stage.FactFactTable.Table.sql` to the correct folder and replace 'FactTable' with the name of your fact table in both the file name and the code in the file. Adjust it with all columns.

**Note**: All columns except for ‘measures’ must be **NOT NULL**.

## Fact: Stored procedure for stage table
This stored procedure moves data from ‘archive’ to ‘stage’, as described above. In many cases, it may be sufficient to use a DELETE:INSERT approach, but using a MERGE is recommended and allows data to remain in the stage table, thereby optimizing the next load. This stored procedure must not include records from ‘archive’ that are marked as ‘IsDeleted’, and if a MERGE is used, deleted records can automatically be removed from the stage table.

MERGE naturally requires a unique primary key, which is not always the case; if not, a full load from source to EDW must be accepted.

Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Procedures\stage.Insert_FactFactTable.Table.sql` to the correct folder and replace ‘FactTable’ with the name of your fact table in both the file name and in the code in the file. Adjust it with all columns and decide between using MERGE or DELETE/INSERT.

This template includes examples of both DELETE:INSERT and MERGE. Use the one that fits best, or write other code suited to the situation.

It is very important **not** to perform a delta load in this step, as it would fail to catch cases where a previously unknown dimension value has now become known.

The template includes logic to check if `DW_Audit_ID` in ‘archive’ is greater than in ‘stage’, which can determine if an update is necessary. It may be necessary to create an index on the tables to achieve better performance.

## Fact: Fact table
A fact table should be based on the template below. In this example, there is a unique primary key, which is very suitable for MERGE operations, so consider having a primary key (PK) on the table. This is not always the case, which determines the principle of partial, merge, or full load. In this example, a MERGE is performed between ‘stage’ and ‘fact’, thereby handling INSERT, DELETE, and UPDATE efficiently and effectively.

**Note** that all fields except ‘measures’ must be **NOT NULL.**

Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Tables\fact.FactTable.Table.sql` to the correct folder and replace ‘FactTable’ with the name of your fact table in both the filename and the code inside the file. Adjust it with all columns.

To optimize performance, it may be a good idea to consider various indexes on the fact table if delta-load is used. This could be an index on ‘DW_Audit’, or it could also be an index on fields from the source. Therefore, it may be necessary to add fields to the fact table solely for optimizing updates. The same principle applies to the data mart.

## Fact: Stored procedure for fact table
The stored procedure to move data from ‘stage’ to ‘fact’ not only handles the transfer itself but also converts EK keys to SK keys, because the record from the stage table contains the EK key and the DW_ValidDate on the fact, and the EK key must be used to find the correct SK key (surrogate).

Copy the file `..\src\sql\Templates\Procedures\fact.Insert_FactTable.Table.sql` to the correct folder and replace ‘FactTable’ with the name of your fact table in both the filename and the code inside the file.

In some cases, it may be a good idea to include the EK key on the final fact table, but this is the exception. For example, if you want to join the dimension with the fact table at the EK level—such as a dimension with history per year, which also needs to work as a Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD), but also the option to select a specific year on the dimension and see corresponding records for multiple years. In this way, the EK key is used. See the example:

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-1c14fe94-58b9-4b5c-8cae-031f12229818.png) 

The template contains examples of both DELETE:INSERT and MERGE. Perform a search/replace and adjust the code as needed.

The template includes logic to check if DW_Audit_ID is greater in ‘stage’ than in ‘EDW’, which can determine if an update is necessary. It may be necessary to create an index on the tables to achieve better performance.

The stored procedure can be run manually before the SSIS package is created.

path: /Technology & Software/14. KMDBIFW - BI Framework/14.1 Modules/14.1.5 Log/About Log Module
content:
# Introduction

Logging of the SSIS flow is handled by default through the template SSIS packages included in the framework. Therefore, there is no need to manually manage logging in the SQL code. However, if there is a need for more detailed logging, the logging functionality is described below.

[[_TOC_]]

---

# Log table

The log table is located in the management database ’00_LOG’ and is named ’dbo.Log’. Its contents might look as follows:

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-04c8ba1e-a118-4e85-94db-b268adb8c05e.png) 

The table is populated exclusively via stored procedures, which are also located in the same database.

| Stored Procedure | Parameters/Usage | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **dbo.StartLog** | Project, PackageName, TaskName, SourceSystem | Returns an `Audit_ID` used to call `EndLog`. Can be used as `ParentAudit_ID` to link logs in a parent/child relationship. Supports nested logs by managing multiple `Audit_ID`s. |
| **dbo.EndLogError** | `Audit_ID`, Error message | Closes the log with status “Error” and records the error message. |
| **dbo.EndLogOK** | `Audit_ID`, `Change` (int) – number of Insert/Delete/Update operations | Closes the log with status “OK” and logs the number of changes. The template procedure automatically handles and returns the `Change`. |
| **dbo.EndLogOkDeleteIfNoChildren** | Same as `EndLogOK` | Works like `EndLogOK` but deletes the log if no child logs exist. Useful if no action was actually performed. |

Calls to the stored procedures are made by creating a synonym like this in the EDW database:

```
CREATE SYNONYM [management].[StartLog] FOR [00_LOG].[dbo].[StartLog]
    
CREATE SYNONYM [management].[EndLogError] FOR [00_LOG].[dbo].[EndLogError]
    
CREATE SYNONYM [management].[EndLogOK] FOR [00_LOG].[dbo].[EndLogOK]
    
CREATE SYNONYM [management].[EndLogOKDeleteIfNoChildren] FOR [00_LOG].[dbo].[EndLogOKDeleteIfNoChildren]
```
    
# Logging in an SSIS Package

Below is an example of an SSIS package that handles logging. All SSIS packages are built in the same way with a 'StartLog', an 'EndLog', and an 'ErrorLog'. This ensures logging is automatically managed without extra effort. It requires always starting from an existing package or a template.

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-bab6279c-f4a2-4690-83cf-b0679c5a2b24.png) 

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-a38a68a0-2b19-4d8a-b44e-00b5c57d7c29.png) 

StartLog: At each start log, a unique ‘DW_Audit’ number is generated by calling the stored procedure dbo.StartLog. This DW_Audit number is kept by the SSIS package and passed along to the ‘EndLog’ or ‘ErrorLog’.

Flow: All records that are inserted or updated are stamped with the ‘DW_Audit’ as part of the standard interface required in the called stored procedures. This allows you to directly join the ‘DW_Audit’ field on the data with the corresponding ‘Id’ column in the Log table to track when data was created or if errors occurred.

EndLog: The stored procedure ‘EndLog’ is called with the same ‘DW_Audit’, allowing the log to be ‘closed’ with a status mark (Ok or Error) and the number of affected records, which is also part of the standard interface from the stored procedures in the flow to return the count of records.

ErrorLog: Called if the SSIS package fails using the ‘DW_Audit’ generated at StartLog. An error message is retrieved, which the SSIS package captures by default and sends to the log table.

ParentID:
Note that SSIS main packages work with a ‘ParentID’ (see figure below). In a main package, a ‘StartLog’ is called which generates a ‘DW_Audit’ number that is then called the ‘ParentID’. This ‘ParentID’ is used in corresponding ‘ErrorLog’ and ‘EndLog’ calls and is forwarded to child packages as the column ‘DW_ParentID’.

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-e34693ed-820a-4a4d-a63a-b85d5c94d047.png) 

This provides an opportunity to batch the execution, which offers a great advantage for reporting by enabling analysis of the entire job runs, such as ‘EDW_Oekonomi’ or ‘DSA_SD’, etc. Below is an example of a batch job (ID 13126) that has moved a series of tables from EDW to the Datamart within the finance area. The difference between the ‘starttime’ and ‘endtime’ on the last row with ID 13126 represents the total time taken by the rows above that share this ‘parentid’.

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-677f5460-e29d-4755-b9b1-78c74df8f488.png) 

# Error Handling / Job Execution
This section describes what happens when a main SSIS package is executed and fails. Generally, all main packages run in multiple threads – typically 4. The principle is that the main package fails if just one step fails, but the failure does not occur immediately since multiple threads are running concurrently. For example, if an error occurs in thread 3, threads 1, 2, and 4 will continue to run to completion, but the entire main package will ultimately fail and must be rerun after the error is addressed.

The code that triggers the failure will perform a rollback according to standard error handling in stored procedures.

Main packages, such as those that first build dimensions and then fact tables, will execute the dimension steps first. If those fail, the fact tables will not be created.
SQL jobs typically run with steps that reflect the layers in the architecture (DSA, EDW, DM). This method ensures that the flow does not proceed on error, and the next layer will always remain intact.

Below is an example of how errors are logged to the log table. It indicates which SSIS project it concerns, which flow, and includes an error message.

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-360a21a0-2cca-4b00-9394-dd94a3a919c5.png) 

# Reporting from the Log
It is possible to build a reporting layer on the log table. The database ‘00_Log’ contains several views that can be used for analysis and reporting both from Business Objects and via a cube in tools such as TARGIT. The following views are available:

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-f80d5355-2b9c-4c81-9329-94efbc31e042.png) 

This exposes log data to help visualize errors and performance issues. It is also possible from frontend tools to create alerts and reports that are sent automatically — not only when errors occur. Below is an example of such a report. The first figure is an overview of SQL jobs, and the second is a more detailed overview with SSIS projects.

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-b3e28a0c-ac4e-483e-89bc-73e8d7f439b3.png) 

![==image_0==.png](/.attachments/==image_0==-3505b2b2-26ae-4d39-bf4a-0714aa2a84b2.png)

# RPO and RTO

We have several objectives with different priorities. We want them all handled within 48 hours, but they have different priorities.

| Priority | Recovery Point Objective | Reasoning | Recovery Time Objective |
|--|--|--|--|
| 1 | Customers using SAAS SAP BO, KMD-hosted SAP BO environment and data-out is able to access data as normal. | We want our customers to able to use their solutions. | 48 hours |
| 2 | Developers are able to log into development environments and perform their tasks. | We want to ensure that our developers are able to do their work. | 48 hours |
| 3 | We are able to load new data from data sources over MSSQL databases to IQ so customers can access it. | We want to update our solutions with new data from the sources, as this is a central service. | 48 hours |
| 4 | Able to perform other tasks regarding management of our environment. | All other servers are of lesser priority. | 48 hours |

path: /Processes/6. Support processes/6.1 Survey and and follow-up
content:
The purpose of this section is to document our work with surveys for support cases.

# Surveys

After a case is closed, a survey is sent to the owner of the case at the customer.

- To what extent are you satisfied with the processing time of your support case? (1-5)
- How satisfied are you with the support you received regarding your recently resolved case? (1-5)
- To what extent do you feel you were kept informed about the status of your support case? (1-5)
- Did you find the communication with KMD to be polite and accommodating? (yes/no)
- Did you feel that your case was closed before you considered it "fully resolved"? (yes/no)

# Follow-up

It is our goal to score 4,5 on average on the questions on a scale of 1 to 5 and 95 % on the "yes/no" questions. We divide our follow-up into "first line support" and "second line support".

We conduct follow-ups once a month with two target groups with JA being responsible.

The first follow-up is for the employees in general. Here we provide a summary of the past months measurements and how things are looking in general. The purpose here is to rive people an impression of how customer satisfaction with our support is developing and to remind everybody that we genuinely care about our customers’ opinions of our support.  

This should be posted in DIMA’s internal news channel through OHG. 

The second follow-up is for management. Here we highlight any trends, customers, teams, or employees we should focus on to improve the results.

This section describes the process we use for handling major breakdowns.

[[_TOC_]]

# What is a major breakdown

A breakdown or service interruption qualifies as a major when 25 % of our customers experience this breakdown in some way.

If this is a platform component, the process is handled by Support & Architecture. If this is a specific solution, the process is handled by the corresponding domain team. If it is unclear, this defaults to Support & Architecture until it is clarified where it belongs.

A breakdown or service interruption is classified as **major** when **25% or more of our customers** are affected.
*   If the issue involves a **platform component**, the process is handled by **Support & Architecture**.
*   If the issue is related to a **specific solution**, the corresponding **domain team** is responsible.
*   If unclear, **Support & Architecture** takes ownership until the responsible team is identified.

# Process

## Step 1: Appoint a Coordinator

**Purpose:**  

Ensure a single person is responsible for overseeing the entire process.

**Principles:**
*   The Coordinator is selected from a predefined pool, preferably not involved in the technical troubleshooting.
    - **Support & Architecture**: KMK, MQH, JA or AYH
    - **Administrative**: SNS, LHX or OCG
    - **Welfare**: TKT
*   The Coordinator ensures the process is followed, delegates tasks, follow up on all important tasks and may adapt the process if needed (e.g., skip customer communication if the issue is invisible to them, or delay restoration to gather critical insights).

**Actions:**
*   Announce the initiation of the process in the team’s dedicated channel.
*   Use this channel for all further updates and communication.

* * *

## Step 2: Communication

**Purpose:**  

Inform customers and internal stakeholders early about the issue, our response, and when to expect the next update.

**Principles:**
*   Early communication is essential—inform before deep problem-solving begins.
*   Always include the **next update time** and stick to it.

**Actions:**
*   The Coordinator informs customers communication about the situation, our response, and the next update using the communication template (https://kmd.service-now.com/now/nav/ui/classic/params/target/kb_view.do%3Fsysparm_article%3DKB0015485). This is done using Service Now.
*   The Coordinator informs DIMA and relevant colleagues using the same template by mail. Default is all of DIMA.
*   The Coordinator informs all stakeholders when the issue is considered resolved.

* * *

## Step 3: Identify the Problem

**Purpose:**  

Determine the problem and how to fix it.

**Principles:**
*   Focus solely on identifying the issue and the fix — no extended analysis at this stage.

**Actions:**
*   Identify the cause and the fix to restore normal operations.
*   Remember to communicate to internal and external stakeholders.
*   Create incident with oXya or Kyndryl as soon as we now enough about the situation.

**Platform specific:**

Actions specific for a platform breakdown.

*   If a MSSQL server has broken down, verify if it has any globale modules. This could mean the impact goes beyond the customers on the specific server.

* * *

## Step 4: Restore Normal Operations

**Purpose:**  

Return all affected customers to normal operation as quickly as possible.

**Principles:**
*   Prioritize restoration over analysis or documentation.

**Actions:**
*   Restore services for all affected customers.
*   Verify successful restoration through relevant method.
*   Inform all relevant parties.
*   Begin collecting information for learning and improvement once services are restored.

* * *

## Step 5: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) & Improvement Initiatives

**Purpose:**  

Learn from the incident to prevent recurrence and improve future response.

**Actions:**
*   All involved gather relevant information for analysis.
*   The Coordinator schedules an evaluation meeting within one week.

**Evaluation Meeting Agenda:**
1.  Brief overview of the incident and response.
2.  Discussion of key learnings.
3.  Agreement on improvement actions and responsible persons.
4.  Coordinator assigns follow-up responsibilities.

Use this template for the meeting: [Evaluation Meeting template.docx](https://kmddk.sharepoint.com/:w:/s/DIMALG-365/EWQVyJJA_SpBo-DW7ySnVv4BpUxwAZ2svo50ZQ4IerfGHw?e=OCLemC)
Place the filled out template here: [Break down evaluations](https://kmddk.sharepoint.com/:f:/s/DIMALG-365/EqPXr6pFkl5BjtU04Ukt8kUB20XI3pgObXcrIcQWp53NkQ?e=NUHjZv)

# The Role of the Dedicated Primary Contact Person (DPCP)

A **DPCP** is a designated individual within the Administrative Domain Team who serves as the main point of contact for a select group of strategically important customers. The purpose of the DPCP role is to strengthen long-term relationships, ensure continuity, and provide proactive coordination of complex or high-priority matters.

The DPCP:
*   Acts as the customer’s go-to person for significant contractual or technical change requests.
*   Coordinates internally to ensure smooth execution and follow-up.
*   Focuses on building trust and maintaining a high level of customer satisfaction.
*   Does not replace sales or support roles, but complements them by handling cross-functional coordination and relationship management.

The list of affected customers can be found on its own tab in the SUPPORT-INFO sheet on the shared DIMA site:
[SUPPORT-INFO ver. 03.xlsx](https://kmddk.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/Dima-365/Eaq7nvh-NRVIvwg_fCg546sB10tVPkdIH2BOa1eAflboeA?e=sKdeHn&nav=MTVfezM5MDAxNTA1LTEwM0YtNDVENy1CMDc0LTU0QjUyOUUwNTYxRX0)

This role was previously referred to as **SPOC (Single Point of Contact)** but has been renamed to better reflect its strategic nature and to not conflict with similar terms used in the Sales Team.

content:
# Introduction

This page outlines the current status and structure of an ongoing CI/CD pipeline setup in Azure DevOps. The purpose of this pipeline is to automate the provisioning of Azure infrastructure using Bicep templates. The pipeline setup is currently a work in progress in the playground DevOps, if do not have permissons to access the repository, reach out to @<49DA450B-1964-6459-8C6D-AE9EAA1ED5D6>.

Direct link to the repository: [kmdbi.cicd.global - Repos](https://dev.azure.com/DIMALGSPlayground/MMP%20testproject/_git/kmdbi.cicd.global).

---

## Purpose

The main goal of this CI/CD pipeline is to enable consistent, repeatable, and version-controlled deployment of infrastructure components across environments through Azure DevOps.

## Pipeline Overview

The pipeline is composed of several stages and reusable YAML templates. These components work together to automate the infrastructure deployment process using Bicep.

#### 1. Variable Configuration

The `variables.yml` file contains shared variables such as:
*   `location` – defines the Azure region
    
*   `environment` – used to distinguish between dev/test/prod
    
*   `resourcePrefix` – standard prefix applied to resource names for consistency
    
These variables are referenced throughout the pipeline to ensure standardized naming and configuration.

#### 2. Infrastructure Deployment Job

The core deployment logic resides in a reusable job template: `deploy-job.yml`, which takes care of orchestrating the deployment tasks.
*   It utilizes a `bicep` task defined in `deploy-bicep-task.yml` to deploy Azure resources using the `main.bicep` file.
    
*   The `deploy-infra.yml` pipeline defines how the job is invoked and how parameters are passed.
    
This modular structure improves maintainability and reusability across different pipelines or environments.

#### 3. Bicep Template

The `main.bicep` file describes the Azure resources to be provisioned, such as:
*   Azure Key Vault
    
*   Resource Group(s)
    
*   Potentially other infrastructure components (WIP)
    

## Current Status

The pipeline is under active development and serves as a foundation for future expansion. The structure is in place, and initial tests show that core deployments are functioning as intended.
However, progress is currently blocked due to a permission issue: **I am unable to grant myself "Contributor" rights to the Azure Key Vault** via the Azure Portal. This prevents successful resource creation that requires elevated access.

### Next Steps

*   Resolve Key Vault permissions issue
    
*   Expand `main.bicep` to include additional infrastructure components
    
*   Add environment-specific configurations
    
*   Implement post-deployment validation steps
    
If you have any questions to the work so far, reach out to @<009D3411-D76A-62A1-93CF-BE37CE87D54A>.

# Introduction
This page provide you with a guide on how to set up git on a given host like your personal PC. It also describes how setup GIT in vs code, from where you can run git commands from your local repository towards the remote repository on Azure DevOps.

## Request access to CA-Persona-Developers
If you are going to interact with GIT from KMDPFOSAP domain, then you need access to CA-Persona-Developers. This can be done here: CA-Persona-Developers https://myaccess.microsoft.com/@KMDDK.onmicrosoft.com#/access-packages/available.

Se more info on this topic here: https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_wiki/wikis/KMDBI.wiki/10464/10.1-Device-based-login

## Install git
First make sure that GIT is installed on your host. Go to this page and download version to windows: https://git-scm.com/downloads

Recommend to download **Git for Windows/x64 Setup**.

Just do a default installation of git with recommended configurations.

Note: if you only going to interact with git from KMDPFOSAP domain, this step can be skipped as this is already done on the relevant app servers.

## Clone first repo to local repo
To clone your first repo from remote to local follow these steps:
1. Go to https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_git/ . If you not already have access to Azure DevOps, follow this guideline: https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_wiki/wikis/KMDBI.wiki/10198/16.2-Access-to-DevOps-(timeregristation-and-projectmanagement)
2. Find your relevant repo from dropdown
3. Clone repo using VS code (alternatively use command line)
![image.png](/.attachments/image-f67cd5cf-23c5-4a69-a76d-4937c7262062.png)
4. Follow prompt in vs code and select destination for local repo.
5. First time you will be prompt for login, use you @kmd.dk account. 

## Make your first commit to remote repo
You might experience some issue first time you will do a commit, then follow these steps.
1. Do change to any file with can be pushed to remote branch.
2. Add commit message (recommend using [github copilot](https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_wiki/wikis/KMDBI.wiki/9087/12.-GitHub-CoPilot) for auto generate commit messages)
2. Commit and sync in vs code
![image.png](/.attachments/image-5a7befd5-267c-4d76-905f-bb7be0c99860.png)
3. It will then prompt you about configuring username and email. Run the following commands in a terminal:
   - `git config user.email "<email>"`  
   - `git config user.name "<full name>"`  
Now it should be in place.

## Errors about terminal not recognizing git commands
If you terminal does not recognize git commands used in ex. user configurations, and you get an error like:
```
git : The term 'git' is not recognized as a name of a cmdlet, function, script file, or executable program.
Check the spelling of the name, or if a path was included, verify that the path is correct and try again.
```

Then please follow these steps:
1. Restart VS Code after installing Git.  
2. Run the following in a terminal: `echo $env:PATH`  
3. Check the output for the path: `C:\Program Files\Git\cmd`  
4. If the above path is not in the environment variable, add it manually (it should normally be set during installation).  
5. Restart VS Code.  
6. Run `echo $env:PATH` again to ensure the environment variable is set.  
7. Run the following in a terminal to verify that Git commands work: `git --version`  
8. Then configure your username and email by running the following commands:  
   - `git config user.email "<email>"`  
   - `git config user.name "<full name>"`  

You should now be able to commit to your remote branch.

This page details important agreements with oXya regarding our collaboration.

_This is a work in progress!_

[[_TOC_]]

# Restart SAP BO and IQ

We have made the agreement with oXya that they are normally the ones who restart SAP BO and IQ but we can do it if we first do the following information:

- Write it in the common Teams chat.
- Write an email to kmd-dima@oxya.com

In this communication we should state:

- What servers or services we are restarting
- Why we are doing it.

# Root Cause Analysis

We have agreed the following process regarding RCAs on the 28th of February by mail:

All P1 incidents should automatically trigger a Root Cause Analysis. oXya will initiate that analysis on their own initiative without KMDs explicit request. It is implicit that if a P1 occurred, KMD want a Root Cause Analysis. If it takes longer than three weeks to perform, KMD will be informed of the expected delivery date.

# Usage of detailed logging

By mail on 05.03.35 we agreed to use detailed logging in SAP BO for P1 and P2 incidents.

This is done as follows:
  
* Login using Enterprise ID (Administrator) and increasing the tracing level of CMS to High.
* Change tomcat logging level from "Info" to "DEBUG" on server and do a rolling restart of tomcat services on App 1 and App 2.
* Reproduce the issue, capture logs and analyze/share with SAP.

#Follow-Up Principles - **Follow-up date** is set 7 calendar days ahead after customer contact. - Exception: If an agreement or communication with the customer states no updates for a longer period (e.g. if we know it will be 4 weeks before we hear from SD, a follow-up date should be set accordingly). - If multiple events occur simultaneously: **Combine them into one comment**. - If a question is asked to the customer: Set follow-up date 7 days ahead. If no response, follow up again. - **The follow-up date indicates the latest time for customer update**, but communication is encouraged earlier if relevant updates are available.

#Templates for Customer Communication / Eksempler på hvad man kan svare ##Case forwarded from 1st line / Modtagelse i 1st line Hej Jeg har sendt din henvendelse videre til en kollega, som kan hjælpe dig videre. Du hører fra os snarest muligt. Med venlig hilsen --- ## Case received in 2nd line / Modtagelse i 2nd line Hej Jeg har modtaget din sag og forventer at kigge på den senest XXX Så snart jeg har kigget på din sag, vil du modtage en ny status fra mig. Med venlig hilsen --- ##Change of responsible person / Flytning til anden ansvarlig Hej Jeg har netop overtaget din sag og vil fremover være den ansvarlige for sagen. Du er meget velkommen til at kontakte mig, hvis du har spørgsmål eller behov for opfølgning. Du kan forvente at høre fra mig snarest, når jeg har haft mulighed for at sætte mig ind i sagen. Med venlig hilsen --- ## Involvement of third party / Inddragelse af 3.part Hej Jeg er jo i fuld gang med at undersøge din sag. I den forbindelse har jeg nu bedt om hjælp/information fra (**leverandør/anden KMD Afdeling**). Så snart jeg hører fra (**leverandør/anden KMD Afdeling** så får du en opdatering fra mig. Med venlig hilsen --- ## Phone or Teams meeting with customer / Telefon eller Teams møde Hej Som opfølgning på vores **samtale/chat**, vil jeg her kort opsummere hvad vi drøftede: * **Indsæt kort opsummering af hvad der er blevet drøftet** * **Indsæt eventuelle aftaler** Med venlig hilsen --- ##Case forwarded to another KMD department (outside DIMA) / Flytning til anden KMD afdeling (udenfor DIMA) Hej Jeg har sendt din sag videre til **(afdelingens navn**), da **(indsæt forklaring)** Mine kollegaer hos **(afdelingens navn**) er orienteret om, at din sag er blevet sendt videre til dem. Du vil høre nærmere fra dem, når de har haft mulighed for at se på sagen. Med venlig hilsen --- ## Case changed to Service Request (change request/ Ændring til Service Request Hej Da din sag vedrører (**indsæt forklaring,**) vurdere vi, at sagen ikke er en supportsag, men et ændringsønske. Vi beholder sagen her i systemet...**bla bla bla** Med venlig hilsen --- ##Case closed / Sagen afsluttes Hej På baggrund af [**indsæt forklaring**) tillader jeg mig at lukke sagen. Mener du at sagen ikke er afsluttet, kan du tilføje en kommentar direkte i din sag på KMD Serviceportalen ved at klikke på nedenstående link. Har vi ikke hørt fra dig indenfor 5 arbejdsdage lukkes sagen automatisk. Skulle du efter 5 arbejdsdage opleve at sagen ikke er løst, er du velkommen til at oprette en ny sag. Med venlig hilsen --- ## No update to customer in 7 days / Opfølgning på sag Hej Der er følgende opdatering på din sag: Med venlig hilsen

This page describes how this FLIS Tabular Workflow is setup and executed.

**Server Setup**

We have 3 tabular instances to process the tabular FLIS cubes
- KDIPMSSDB03\Tabular
- KDIPMSSDB04\Tabular
- KDIPMSSDB05\Tabular
These three instances are running every weekday (monday-Friday) between 12 and 18:15
Started and stopped vis a windows Task scheduler job on the three servers

One instance that holds the tabular cubes towards the customers

- KDIPMSSDB08\Tabular

On all the serverinstances the user `kmdpfosap\service_bicubes` has been added as owner to instance

This page describes how the setup works and how it is managed.

**User Setup**

We have one user to process and run the scripts 

`kmdpfosap\service_bicubes`


This is the setup:

On KDIPMSSDB03,KDIPMSSDB04 and KDIPMSSDB05 create credential and proxy

```
USE [master]
GO
CREATE CREDENTIAL [c_service_bicubes] WITH IDENTITY = N'kmdpfosap\service_bicubes', SECRET = N'See Password in Secret Server'
GO

USE [msdb]
GO
EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_add_proxy @proxy_name=N'p_service_bicubes',@credential_name=N'c_service_bicubes', 
		@enabled=1
GO
EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_grant_proxy_to_subsystem @proxy_name=N'p_service_bicubes', @subsystem_id=3
GO
EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_grant_proxy_to_subsystem @proxy_name=N'p_service_bicubes', @subsystem_id=12
GO
```


```
on KDIPMSSDB01

Add kmdpfosap\service_bicubes to KMDFLISOLAP database as dbowner
Add kmdpfosap\service_bicubes to GLOBAL_00_LOG database as dbreader,dbwriter

```
On all SQL SERVERS KDIPMSSDB01 to KDIPMSSDB14
Add kmdpfosap\service_bicubes to all *FLIS* Databases with read rights
```


```
On KDIPMSSDB03,KDIPMSSDB04 and KDIPMSSDB05

Make sure kmdpfosap\service_bicubes has full control over "C:\temp"
Make sure kmdpfosap\service_bicubes has full control over "F:\OLAP\Backup"

All output from the script are logged in GLOBAL_00_LOG database on kdipmssdb01 and on each processing server in the folder c:\temp\ in the file MoveSSASDBlog_yyyymmdd.log.  A new file is generated everyday and should be cleaned every 30 days.

#Intro
Denne guide vil vise dig hvordan du bruger MySQL Workbench med udgangspunkt i nexus.
MySQL Workbench kan bruges til at kigge på kildedata, altså inden vi gør noget ved data i vores systemer. 

#Opret forbindelse til database
Først kan du tilføje en forbindelse til en database. Det gør du ved at trykke på + ikonet. 
![image.png](/.attachments/image-a1a19044-f9b1-4e97-bf60-e37e373b7215.png)
Så vil du se nedenstående pop-up vindue.
![image.png](/.attachments/image-57d9ea25-0624-440b-bd72-3abbe74ea32b.png)
Her skal du indtaste Connection Name, Hostname, Port, Username og Password. Connection Name bestemmer du selv, det kan f.eks. være "851 Aalborg". De resterende oplysninger finder du i Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio (MSSMS). Du skal have adgang til kunden via prodsiteportal (Indsæt guide til prodsiteportal) og derefter finde kunden i MSSMS --> åbne DSA --> åbne Views --> select top 1000 rows fra System.v_ProviderString. Så vil du se følgende:
![image.png](/.attachments/image-37e95d77-a13d-4912-be65-58fcace6ef8e.png)
Kopier feltet under "MSSProviderString" ud, så du kan se alle oplysninger. Nu kan du kopiere hostname, port, username og password over i pop-up vinduet "Setup New Connection". 
Når disse er indtastet, så kan du trykke på "test connection" for at se om forbindelsen virker. Hvis du får besked om at forbindelsen er succesfuld, så kan du trykke på "OK". Nu har du oprettet din første forbindelse i MySQL Workbench. 

#Kig i databasen
Hvis du vil kigge på kildedata for en kunde, så skal du trykke på din connection i home viewet i MySQL Workbench.
![image.png](/.attachments/image-f6c65091-2d10-4daa-add7-4f0780435a39.png)
Så skal du vælge "omsorgsocial" på listen i venstre side. 
![image.png](/.attachments/image-064d91ff-3119-4963-9da2-6d08fed29968.png)
Herunder kan du vælge dén tabel, som du vil kigge på. Du kan f.eks. højreklikke på "patient" tabellen og vælge "Select rows - Limit 1000". Så åbnes en query, som udtrækker de 1000 første rækker af patient tabellen. Data kan ses under querien. 
![image.png](/.attachments/image-a414507a-0a95-45f7-afc6-e05145f86816.png)
Så kan du rette din query til, så du får dé data ud som ønsket.

content:
Important !!!
=====       
Dynamic Time will only work with complete and unbroken date dimensions

The example below, shows a setup where the date dimension for 2025 is not complete and several dates (eg. 2025-01-01)
![image.png](/.attachments/image-ab0b1681-5cad-43e5-9719-b4c7d9cdf124.png)







Links
=====

[https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188117-Dynamic-Time-Dimension](https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188117-Dynamic-Time-Dimension)
[https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188717-Enabling-Dynamic-Criteria-through-Decorations](https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188717-Enabling-Dynamic-Criteria-through-Decorations)
[https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017289838-Using-Dynamic-Criteria-in-the-TARGIT-client](https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017289838-Using-Dynamic-Criteria-in-the-TARGIT-client)
[https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188437-Enabling-Dynamic-Criteria-through-SSAS](https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188437-Enabling-Dynamic-Criteria-through-SSAS)

Dynamic Time explained
======================

Targit has implemented a functionality for working with a set of predefined dynamic options to the time dimension.
![image.png](/.attachments/image-e0b18e61-d73e-492b-a04b-24b5f8a76265.png)

The functionality can be implemented directly in a SSAS model (if it is OLAP, not Tabular) or it can be handled through Targits decorations.

If you want to know more about implementing in OLAP, please read here: [https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188437-Enabling-Dynamic-Criteria-through-SSAS](https://community.targit.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017188437-Enabling-Dynamic-Criteria-through-SSAS)

Decorations in Targit Management
================================

Unfortunately, the following screenshots are in Danish.
Start ‘Manage decorations’
![image.png](/.attachments/image-3e30d3df-0686-43ee-810a-d2862a307ce8.png)

Find the time dimension you want to work with and click the ‘Dynamic time definition’
![image.png](/.attachments/image-0ae661ea-0f41-44cd-891a-c13a211ec42d.png)

Type in the dynamic time specification. It can be helpful to drag in the time hierarchy in a mdx statement to see what syntax you should create:

![image.png](/.attachments/image-3cb1a74e-7247-4532-a7f5-87fdbfa51fd1.png)

This line translates into the following definition:
&[<YYYY>].&[<KQ YYYY>].&[<YYYYMM>].&[<W>]
& means key (instead of name)
&[<YYYY>] = 2020 (YY=20),
&[<KQ YYYY>], ‘K’ is a constant, Q is replaced with quarter number, YYYY= 2020
&[<YYYYMM>], key for month (202007)
&[<W>], weeknumber

Targit also need to know what the levels of the hierarki, is translated to, so please fill in the third tab as well
![image.png](/.attachments/image-7413b153-f560-4f8f-9dea-1a1ffc7662fc.png)

This should ensure a proper working Dynamic Time

# Template-Based CI/CD Framework (Azure DevOps)

## Overview
This framework standardizes how CI/CD pipelines are written in Azure DevOps by splitting responsibilities into **stages**, **jobs**, and **tasks**, each defined in **dedicated YAML templates**.

### Installationstypes
Currently this framework only support the following installationtype:
- psm: Powershell Modules
- psservice: PS executables installed as a windows service
- sqlproj: SQLProj database projects.
- bim: Tabular model.bim projects.

All other installationtypes are still managed by the modulecoretool.

### Key Principles

#### Separation of concerns
- **Stages**: Orchestration, parameterization and dependency management between jobs
- **Jobs**: Orchestration, parameterization and dependency management between tasks and linkage to environments  
- **Tasks**: logic execution

#### Centralized PowerShell logic
- All execution logic lives in a dedicated PowerShell module called **kmdbips.cicd.global** 
- YAML tasks wrap these functions

#### Reusability
- Templates for tasks, jobs, and variables are shared across pipelines

#### Dynamic flexibility
- Supports blacklisting (jobs/stages) and parameterized imports

#### Self-hosted agents
- Everything runes on a self hosted agent, for it to have access to the on-prem ressources.

#### Environments
- Environments to help manage deployment targets, apply approvals, track history, and visualize releases across the different hosts in the KMDPFOSAP domain.

#### Artifact feed
- Artifact feed to store stable build versions of any modules to install in production

#### KMDBISITE/Admin portal
- Release management, configuration and master data management in one centralized web app allowing automation of full deployments and scaling.

#### Azure Key vault
- All credentials are stored in Azure Key Vault and injected in pipelines when needed. 

---
## Execution Flow
The illustration below provides an overview of the whole CICD flow and the components that is used within.

![cicdArchitecture.png](/.attachments/cicdArchitecture-8887c12c-4a55-4635-bb91-e1c9a365d615.png)
Find a interactive visual of this diagram [here](https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_git/kmdbi.cicd.global?path=/cicdArchitecture.drawio.png). 

### Execution Flow (CI Example)
1. **Stage (CI)** → orchestrates validation jobs → called from individuel modules.
2. **Job** → cleans directories, resolves PS module path, invoke powershell tasks.
3. **Tasks** → invoke PowerShell functions, like:
   - Update WinSW XML  
   - Stage files  
   - Fetch secrets from Key Vault  
   - Deploy to target servers  
   - Publish pipeline artifacts

Read more about the CI flow [here](https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_wiki/wikis/KMDBI.wiki/11083/CI-pipelines).

### Execution Flow (CD Example)
1. **Stage (CD) orchestrator** → takes installation queue from admin portal and triggers a deployment pipeline (new independent pipeline). This orchestrator is triggered every 5 min from mon-sat 7-20 and checks for installations in the queue. This orchestrator only triggers deployment pipeline (cd.deployment) if any installations are queued.
2. **Stage (CD) deployment** → Triggered by orchestrator with installation parameters like, installationID, InstallationType, CustomerNo and Deployment server.
3. **Job** → based on InstallationType suited job template is initiated. This job contains all relevant tasks for deploying the given release.
4. **Tasks** → invoke PowerShell functions, like:
   - Downloading release artifact  
   - Extracts relevant content
   - Fetch secrets from Azure Key Vault  
   - Deploys release on target host

Read more about the CD flow [here](https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_wiki/wikis/KMDBI.wiki/11064/CD-pipelines).

---

## Benefits
- Consistency across pipelines  
- Centralized logic in PowerShell module  
- Modular, composable templates  
- Dynamic blacklisting & parameterization  

---

## Best Practices
1. Keep orchestration in **YAML**, logic in **PowerShell**  
2. Always use **task templates**, never inline PS in jobs  
3. Use **variable templates** for shared configuration  
4. Apply **blacklists** to skip dynamically  
5. Validate new PS functions in **test pipelines** before production integration

# Introduction
This page contain information on how the Admin Portal that is currently used for release management is used in the new Azure DevOps setup.

## Configuration
Under configurations in the Admin Portal new entries have been added to the 'InstallationType' and 'ModuleType' tables.

### InstallationType
Since the Azure DevOps pipeline covers installation of new installation types compared to what we previously had, four new installationTypes have been added:
- BIM: Installation of tabular models in .bim fileformat
- SQLPROJ: Installation of SQLPROJ modules.
- PSM: Installation of PowerShell modules.
- PSSERVICE: Installation of PowerShell Service modules.

**BIM**
*   A `.bim` file is essentially a JSON representation of a tabular model.
*   It stores the full definition of the model, including all tables, columns, measures, relationships, and metadata.
*   BIM files are often used for version control, deployment, and automation.

**SQLPROJ**
*   The `.sqlproj` file itself is XML, describing the structure, included files, build settings, and references.
*   You can build the project to generate a DACPAC (Data-tier Application Package) file.
    *   The DACPAC is a portable package representing the database schema, which can be deployed to any SQL Server instance.

**PSM**
A PowerShell module is essentially a package of reusable PowerShell code—functions, cmdlets, variables, and other resources—that can be **loaded into a PowerShell session to extend its capabilities. It’s the way PowerShell organizes and distributes functionality.

**PSSERVICE**
To install PowerShell as a service the winsw libery. WinSW is a lightweight tool that allows you to run any executable, script, or program as a Windows service, including PowerShell scripts. It essentially “wraps” your script so Windows can treat it like a proper service.

It works bye:

*   Download WinSW → Usually `WinSW-x64.exe`. This file is stored on the artifact feed and downloaded in the CI pipeline and then added to the release artifact.
    
*   Create an XML configuration file (same name as the executable, e.g., `MyService.xml`) specifying:
    *   The executable to run (`powershell.exe`)
    *   The arguments (path to your script)
    *   Startup behavior (`auto`, `manual`)
    *   Logging location
    *   Restart policies on failure

### ModuleType
To manage these new installation type two new module types have been added:
- TABULAR: Tabular module that contains .bim file.
- KMDBIPS: PowerShell module, that contains both the powershell module, but can also contain the powershell service, if some of the functions have to be installed as a service (ex. the new worker for job orchestration).

**Tabular**
The Tabular module have to contain the following files and folders:
- devops
  - module_var.yaml: Containing variables for CI pipeline.
  - tabular_ci.yaml: Containing the pipeline yaml script, which the ci piplines is based upon.
- src/tabular
  - .bim file: The definition of the tabular database project.

**KMDBIPS**
The KMDBIPS module have to contain the following files and folders:
- devops
  - module_var.yaml: Containing variables for CI pipeline.
  - powershell_ci.yaml: Containing the pipeline yaml script, which the ci piplines is based upon.
- bin
  - pull_includes.ps1: reuse.kmdbips.global which contains reuse scripts to run and handle the moduletype.
- private
  - any internal functions supporting the public functions displayed in the powershell module.
- public
  - containing all functions that can be used from the powershell module.
- .psd1: Metadata describing the module (version, author, dependencies, exported commands).
- .psm1: Typically a single `.psm1` file containing functions.
- Initialize-Module.ps1: initializes module and changes the manifest according to module content.
- psservice (optional): To install powershell function as a service:
  - <Function to call>.ps1: The function which the service is based upon.
  - params.ps1: param file that is used when starting the service.

## Azure DevOps Configurations
This is a new category within the admin portal, this category contains tables that is used in the CICD pipelines. The content within these tables are typically configurations for the different modules that is managed by the Azure DevOps piplines.

Some of the new tables within this category are:
- Tabular Roles: Mapping ModuleName, CustomerName together with role permissions on the tabular database. It is used in the CD deployment pipelines for installation type BIM.
- Application Database: Mapping ModuleName, InstallationType, InstallationServer together with a underlying application database server. Ex. used for new worker on which server it needs to fetch queue information. This is used in the CD deployment pipelines for PSSERVICE modules.

## Secrets
This is also a new category within the admin portal, this category contains tables that is used to fetch secrets from Azure Devops and used within the CICD pipelines.
- Secrets: Contains all relevant secrets within the key vault which can be utilized by the pipeline and parsed to the installed application.
- Secrets mapping: Mapping SecretName with ModuleName, datasource and CustomerName.


## Installation
Nothing have changed in the way a module is added to the release queue. Only thing that has changed is that a new orchestrator is introduced. Previously the modulecoretool was used for orchestrating all installations. Bye the implementation of the CICD pipelines in Azure DevOps, a new orchestrator has been added, read more about it [here](https://dev.azure.com/kmd-dima/KMD.DIMA.LG/_wiki/wikis/KMDBI.wiki/11100/shared.cd.orchestrator). To make sure that the modulecoretool still orchestrates the DSA and DATAAREA modules, a new stored procedure in KMDBISITE has been added. The Azure DevOps orchestrator fetch installation queue info through stored procedure `[install].[GetInstallListDevOps]`, this stored procedure only returns queued installations of installationtype psm, psservice, sqlproj and bim. Also in `[install].[GetInstallList]` which the modulecoretool orchestrator uses, these installationtypes are excluded. Bye doing so it is secured that both applications are not installing the same entries in the queue.

# CD Framework – Template-Based Flow

This CD framework implements a **template-based pipeline design** in Azure DevOps.  
It separates orchestration (stages, jobs) from logic execution (tasks, PowerShell modules), ensuring consistency, modularity, and reuse across projects.

Below is the CD flow described.

![cdFramework.png](/.attachments/cdFramework-290f1f32-b94b-4004-a34f-0c0c2a592f94.png)

---

## Overview of Flow

The pipeline is divided into two main layers:

1. **Release orchestrator**  
   - A orchestrator pipeline, that reads the install queue in KMDBISITE every 5 minutes. If any installations queued then it triggers the deployment pipeline. Besides trigger installation it sets the installation to status 'Requested for installation'.
   - If there are multiple entries in the installation queue, then it triggers all of them for installation. It groups the queued installations based on CustomerNo, DeploymentHost and InstallationModuleName, and initiates the `cd.deployment` pipeline for each group. By grouping it this way makes it possible to set dependencies in installation order, if there are multiple installationstypes in each module.
   - The orchestrator fetch installation queue info through stored procedure `[install].[GetInstallListDevOps]`, this stored procedure only returns queued installations of installationtype psm, psservice, sqlproj and bim. Also in `[install].[GetInstallList]` which the modulecoretool orchestrator uses, these installationtypes are excluded. Bye doing so it is secured that both applications is not installing the same entries in the queue.
  - The yaml files making out the orchestrator is also part of the kmdbi.cicd.global repository, and has the same layers and approach as the actual deployment pipeline.

2. **Framework - cd.deployment (kmdbi.cicd.global)**  
   - Provides shared templates for stages, jobs, and tasks.  
     - Stages: contain a prefixed number of jobs.  
     - Jobs: contain a prefixed number of tasks.  
     - Tasks: contain a prefixed operation.  
   - Contains the centralized PowerShell module (`kmdbips.cicd.global`) with reusable functions.  
     By splitting the actual operations into a PowerShell module, operations can also be executed directly from a local host, bypassing the Azure Pipeline orchestration. This also prevents vendor lock-in with Azure DevOps.


---

Within the subpages to this wiki, you will find relevant info on the release orchestrator and the cd.deployment pipeline.
